description: We are creating a CLPS landing site browser. It will inform users on the benefits of a certain landing site, as well as the sky chart %of time in sunlight and with earth visible. It will also inform users on the slope, elevation and temperature range. You will be able to choose a lander and payload from real CLPS landers with their specs, choose a landing site that works for the lander. It will also have the ability to visualize the lander and compare it to other chosen landing sites/crafts.
summary: Lunarcy is a landing site navigator that helps scientists choose where to send an uncrewed lander to study water ice on the Moon. Users enter their mission needs: dates, how much sunlight and Earth contact they require, solar power, maximum slope, and how close they want to be to a likely ice deposit. Lunarcy searches the whole Moon, ranks the landing regions that meet those needs, and explains why each one was picked. For a chosen site it shows the Sun and Earth against the real terrain horizon, power and communication timelines, the best landing dates, and a 3D view that places a solar array and a communications tower and maps a drivable route toward the nearest ice. It is built on NASA data: JPL Horizons for Sun and Earth positions, LRO LOLA elevation for terrain, and LRO Diviner temperatures for cold traps. Finding usable ice matters because it can become drinking water, oxygen and rocket fuel, turning the Moon from a place we visit into a place we can stay. Lunarcy is a 3D globe anyone can explore, from mission planners to students.
details:
Project Details

Paste the text below. It follows the form's questions in order.

What it does. Lunarcy helps a science team choose where to land an uncrewed lander to study water ice on the Moon. There are three ways in:

  • Explore the Moon: spin a 3D globe, browse past and planned landing sites, or click anywhere.
  • Plan a mission: enter dates, minimum sunlight and Earth contact, solar power, maximum slope, and a maximum distance to ice.
  • Learn: short cards and a guided tour on why the lunar poles are so hard to plan for.

How it works.

  • Site search: checks 43,200 cells across the whole Moon (0.5°, about 15 km each) against the mission, then re-checks the best regions against real terrain. It returns ranked regions with a plain-language reason for each pick.
  • Visibility: the Sun and Earth only count as visible when they clear the actual terrain skyline traced from NASA LOLA elevation, not a flat horizon.
  • For each site: a 360° horizon panorama, Sun and Earth elevation and in-view timelines, panel sunlight, best landing dates if the schedule slips, and nearby spots within 3 km.
  • Site plan (3D view): places a solar array where sunlight is highest and a comms tower where Earth is in view longest. It maps a drivable route between them, avoiding ground steeper than 15° (the VIPER rover's limit), and shows the distance to the nearest ice candidate.
  • Ice candidates: 205 named polar craters, rated by permanent shadow (from LOLA terrain), cold traps at or below 110 K (from Diviner), and published evidence. Five craters have published ice evidence: Cabeus, Haworth, Shoemaker, Faustini and Shackleton.

Benefits and impact. Professionals get a fast, explained first screen of landing candidates and a starting layout for power and comms equipment. Students and the public can choose where a Moon mission lands and see why it works. Locally, the route mapping could support Canada's Lunar Utility Vehicle and help teams understand the slopes and distances its components must handle. We hope it also builds on interest sparked by Jeremy Hansen's trip around the Moon.

Tools and languages. Python (FastAPI, NumPy) for the backend and calculations; JavaScript, HTML and CSS with globe.gl and three.js for the 3D globe and site view; plain SVG charts; pytest for tests. Hosted on Microsoft Azure (Ubuntu VM, Caddy for HTTPS). Code: https://github.com/McCEwan/Lunarcy

Creativity. We built a globe instead of a 2D map or spreadsheet, so the tool is enjoyable for professionals and gives students the freedom to pick a landing site themselves. The interface is nearly colourless so the Moon stays the main attraction, and the globe is lit by the real Sun. A title screen with Earth beside the Moon draws people in.

Factors we considered.

  • Data quality: every value is labelled with its source, and estimates are marked as estimates.
  • Terrain resolution: about 237–474 m globally, with about 30 m detail near a chosen site.
  • Ice: mostly predicted from shadow and temperature; only 5 craters have direct or indirect published evidence.
  • Power: modelled per square metre of panel, without panel angle or panel type.
  • Launch windows: not considered.
